text: The acid in your stomach is strong enough to digest meat. Yet it never digests the stomach itself, and the stomach is made of protein too. So what protects it? Let's follow a single bite and find out.

Your digestive system is a long tube from your mouth to the end of your gut, about nine meters when stretched out in an adult. Helper organs, the liver, gallbladder and pancreas, add digestive juices along the way.
The journey starts in the mouth. Your teeth break the food into pieces, and saliva moistens it. Saliva also contains an enzyme that begins to break down starch.
When you swallow, the food enters the esophagus. Waves of muscle squeezing, called peristalsis, push it down to the stomach. That is why you can swallow even upside down.
In the stomach, food is churned with hydrochloric acid and an enzyme called pepsin, which digests protein. The result is a thick liquid called chyme. Food usually stays here for a few hours.

Now the mystery. The stomach wall is covered with a thick layer of mucus, and its cells also release bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid. And the lining is replaced every few days. That is why the stomach does not digest itself.

The chyme then enters the small intestine, which is about six to seven meters long when stretched out. Bile from the liver, stored in the gallbladder, helps digest fat. The pancreas adds enzymes that break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
The inner wall of the small intestine is covered with tiny fingers called villi. They give a huge surface area, so nutrients pass into the blood very efficiently.
What is left moves into the large intestine. It absorbs water and holds trillions of helpful bacteria. What remains is turned into stool and leaves the body.

From mouth to the end, a meal usually takes one to three days. Most of the nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, not the stomach. If you have ongoing stomach pain or blood in your stool, see a doctor.

Remember three things. Food travels through one long tube with help from the liver, gallbladder and pancreas. Mucus protects the stomach from its own acid. And the small intestine does most of the absorbing. Next time, the kidneys: how your body cleans your blood.
